You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

---
name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC grid instances; follow the benchmark's per-turn action protocol and infer transformations from demos.
---

# Continual ARC

1. On every benchmark turn, emit only one protocol action as the entire response: a single valid JSON object on the final line, with no narration, markdown, tool calls, or other text. This also applies after feedback; every turn requires an action. Check action name and fields before sending.
2. Record grid dimensions and budgets, then compare each demo input/output cellwise. Separate transformations by object type and location; identify what changes and what stays invariant, including colors, dimensions, and untouched background. Do not generalize from a single coincidental feature when multiple rules fit.
3. Treat demos and wrong submissions as equal-cost actions. Request a demo only when its likely example can distinguish live hypotheses. Before submitting, state internally one complete rule that accounts for all demos, then apply it to every relevant test object while preserving untouched cells and exact grid dimensions.
4. On incorrect feedback, discard or materially revise the hypothesis: compare it against every demo and identify what the rejected output got wrong. Do not resubmit a small unsupported variation. If uncertainty remains, use a discriminating demo rather than cycling guesses, within the remaining budget.
5. Stop only when the instance reports success/over or the attempt cap is reached; use `finish` only when allowed by the protocol.
